This is Tally. Do their numbers match? By Mia. An entry for the A.I. and Epistemics sprint.

Political speeches lean on numbers. Growth is up. Inflation is down. Each of those numbers comes from an official release, so each one can be checked. But for Nigeria, nobody has put the claims and the official figures side by side in a form others can audit. So the question is simple. When Nigerian leaders quote a statistic, does it match the official figure?

I chose five national addresses before doing any checking. Four by the President, and one by the main opposition candidate, so both sides go through the same procedure. Fifty-nine figures were listed. Forty-nine were checked against the statistics bureau, the central bank, the budget office and others. Forty-six could be scored. Every scored row has a verdict and a link to its source.

Four in five matched. Thirty-seven figures matched the official release, five were close, and four did not match. Every specific growth rate and inflation rate quoted in the five speeches matched exactly.

The biggest misses were two swapped definitions, in the same speech. The President said non-oil exports are now forty-eight percent of exports. The official release shows crude oil at about fifty-three percent, but another thirty-four percent is other petroleum products and gas. Truly non-oil products were about thirteen percent. He also said non-oil revenue had passed twenty trillion naira by August. That was total revenue. Non-oil revenue was under sixteen trillion.

The other errors were more ordinary. A stock market gain quoted from ten days earlier. An oil baseline that belonged to the month before. And the errors ran both ways. Of eight with a clear direction, five helped the speaker and three hurt. Two claims fit no verdict at all. Two official sources give different foreign investment figures, and one debt ratio has no published source.

Can you trust the verdicts? I ran two independent checks. First, a script with no A.I. in it downloaded every source and looked for the recorded numbers. It found all of them in thirty-nine of forty-six rows, and the quoted figures in six more. Second, a different A.I. model coded the rows blind. It agreed on thirty-two of forty-five, and its match rate was seventy-three percent against eighty. So most figures match under either checker. But single verdicts near the boundaries are less reliable, and the second model disputed the revenue finding.

Why is this a Track Four entry? Track Four is about deployment, adoption and impact. Tools that check claims are built and tested where statistics are tidy. This is a test set from a place where they are not. The second check was itself a small deployment test: an off-the-shelf model, handed the right source, still missed one of the two non-oil label swaps. And the barriers to adoption here are concrete. Two official series for the same quantity. Figures with no published source. Source sites that refuse automated readers. The dataset is usable today by fact-checkers and journalists.

What you get is an open dataset, with a source link on every scored row, and a small test set for claim-checking tools in a setting they rarely see. It is small. No human has checked every row. And it does not compare the two speakers. The data, the report and a guide for judges are in the repository. Thank you.
